Software revenue increased five percent. Consulting was effectively flat. But Infrastructure—the division containing IBM's powerful mainframe systems—fell seven percent.

narration: The problem began in the final weeks of June, as companies across the technology industry confronted a new and increasingly expensive reality.
IBM's customers were rapidly changing the order in which they spent their technology budgets.
Money that IBM expected to flow into software and large enterprise agreements was redirected toward servers, storage systems and memory.
This was deeply ironic. IBM had spent years positioning itself as one of the companies best prepared to help businesses enter the artificial-intelligence era.

narration: But the AI boom was creating demand in a specific sequence. Before many companies could deploy new software, they first needed the physical infrastructure capable of running it.

name: Arvind Krishna
title: Chairman, President and CEO of IBM
text: We did not anticipate the magnitude of the capex reprioritization.
narration: IBM had expected supply constraints to influence purchasing decisions. What it misjudged was how quickly—and how aggressively—customers would move their money.

headline: Clients Race to Secure Infrastructure
content_before: Customers were responding to limited hardware availability and the possibility of higher prices.
target_text: Clients shifted quarterly capital spending toward servers, storage and memory purchases.
narration: Customers were attempting to secure supply-constrained equipment before anticipated price increases. For IBM, that shift disrupted buying patterns at the worst possible moment.
And then came the second problem. Numerous large agreements that IBM expected to complete before the end of the quarter simply did not close on schedule.

narration: For an enterprise technology company, a delayed signature can move millions of dollars from one reporting period into the next. When several large deals slip together, the damage becomes visible immediately.

name: Arvind Krishna
title: Chairman, President and CEO of IBM
text: We did not adapt and move quickly enough.
narration: Krishna's conclusion was unusually direct. The external environment had changed—but IBM's own execution had failed to change with it.
He described the supply constraints, the shifting budgets and the cybersecurity concerns affecting clients. Then he made the company's position clear: these were realities, not excuses.
That admission carried unusual weight because IBM is not a young company caught experiencing its first technology cycle.
